research_text:
## 1. API and reported value

`javax.crypto.spec.SecretKeySpec` represents a provider-independent secret key constructed from raw bytes. Oracle says it is useful for keys representable as a byte array without associated key parameters. Its two constructors take either a byte array and algorithm name, or an array slice and algorithm name. The reported `ARCFOUR` is an **algorithm-name value associated with the supplied key material**, not a cipher operation or key value. Oracle lists `ARCFOUR` as the standard name for RC4. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/spec/SecretKeySpec.html))

The supplied CrySL rule allows four spellings: `AES`, `HmacSHA256`, `HmacSHA384`, and `HmacSHA512`. The diagnostic lists additional uppercase, hyphenated, and slash-separated forms, but the rule file itself does not explain that expansion or its matching semantics. Its allow-list is narrower than the general Java API contract. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SecretKeySpec.crysl))

Sources:  
https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/spec/SecretKeySpec.html  
https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html

## 2. Documented usage and remediation

- The constructors copy the supplied bytes. They check basic input and slice conditions, but **do not validate that the bytes form a valid key for the named algorithm**. Oracle recommends an algorithm-specific key specification where its checks are needed, giving `DESKeySpec` as its example. The documentation does not prescribe a universal replacement for every disallowed algorithm. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/spec/SecretKeySpec.html))
- For key generation, Oracle documents `KeyGenerator`, including initialization with a key size and a source of randomness. The constructor documentation does not establish that any particular imported byte array has appropriate provenance or strength. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/KeyGenerator.html))
- AES is an encryption algorithm; HMAC provides message authentication and is not an encryption substitute. Oracle describes AES-GCM as authenticated encryption and says not to reuse a key/IV combination for encryption. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/Mac.html))
- Separately from the `SecretKeySpec` documentation, RFC 7465 prohibits negotiation of RC4 cipher suites in TLS. That is a **TLS-specific** requirement, not a statement that the constructor itself rejects `ARCFOUR`. ([rfc-editor.org](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7465.html?utm_source=openai))

Sources:  
https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/KeyGenerator.html  
https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/security/java-cryptography-architecture-jca-reference-guide.html  
https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7465.html

## 3. Compatibility and migration

`getFormat()` returns `RAW`, and `getEncoded()` returns the key material in a new byte array. The API documentation does **not** define an application’s persisted ciphertext format, wire protocol, or a migration path from ARCFOUR to another algorithm. In particular, merely changing the key’s algorithm label is not a documented ciphertext conversion. Oracle’s JCA guide notes that cipher parameters used for encryption must be made available to the decrypting party. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/spec/SecretKeySpec.html))

`SecretKeySpec` has been present since Java 1.4, but algorithm availability is a separate platform/provider question. For example, Java SE 21 requires AES-GCM with a 128-bit key and the `HmacSHA256` MAC; other algorithms, key sizes, providers, and platform versions require their own documentation checks. The supplied facts do not identify the relevant persisted format, peer protocol, Java version, or provider, so compatibility and a concrete migration path remain unresolved. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/spec/SecretKeySpec.html))

Source:  
https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html

## 4. Exact rule in the supplied source

The matching/event and algorithm-constraint clauses in the source are: ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SecretKeySpec.crysl))

```crysl
SPEC javax.crypto.spec.SecretKeySpec

EVENTS
	c1: SecretKeySpec(keyMaterial, keyAlgorithm);
	c2: SecretKeySpec(keyMaterial, offset, len, keyAlgorithm);
	Con := c1 | c2;

ORDER
	Con

CONSTRAINTS
	keyAlgorithm in {"AES", "HmacSHA256", "HmacSHA384", "HmacSHA512"};
```

- The `SPEC` names `javax.crypto.spec.SecretKeySpec`. The events name `SecretKeySpec` in **two constructor-shaped forms**, with respectively two and four parameters; the declared object types are `byte[]`, `String`, `int`, and `int`. The file does not declare an ordinary method receiver type for these events.
- The rule also states the length and `neverTypeOf` constraints, requires either `preparedKeyMaterial` or `randomized`, and ensures the `speccedKey` and `generatedKey` predicates. It does not explain how `offset` and `len` are bound for the two-argument event or define the provenance predicates.
- **A name-only match is not established by this source.** It does not state whether a detector can match an unrelated method merely because it shares the name, nor does it specify subtype or call-resolution semantics. A definitive yes/no would require evidence beyond this file. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SecretKeySpec.crysl))

The linked URL tracks `master`; this research did not independently verify that its current bytes have the supplied SHA-256 or are the exact revision used by the detector.
